18th century farmstead with what appears to be original outbuildings still intact. Dwelling has been altered, but may contain significant fabric. Early 19th century farmstead. Good architectural example of Victorianised Cape Dutch/vernacular building with rare surviving early fabric. Contributes to a continuing cultural landscape.

20th century swartland werf with some architectural merit. Dwelling is contemporary (post 2005). Outbuildings appear contemporary, but may contain earlier fabric. Requires investigation. Homestead follows traditional werf pattern. Contributes to the continuing cultural landscape.

One of earliest farms granted in this area. Early 18th century farmstead victorianised in the late 19th century. Very good architectural ensemble: number of outbuildings with a high degree of intactness. Some archaeological significance related to LSA occurences. Rare authentic farmstead contributing to the historical characteristics of the continuing cultural landscape.
Structures and outbuildings of some interest. Unfortunate remodelling of barn with inappropriately large openings which detract from the heritage legibility of the structure.

Early/mid 20th century consolidation of portions of Mosselrivier and Lichtenburg. High environmental/contextual significance with regards to its location and proximity to the Mosselrivier. Forms part of a continuing agricultural landscape.
One of the early farms granted in the late 17th century. Good representative example of a swartland farmstead with much historical layering. Feature farmstead within the cultural landscape.
Historically part of Diemersdal farm. Contributes to the environmental and contextual character of the agricultural landscape.

Significant public square associated with the DR Church and a collection of civic buildings. Enhances landmark qualities of the church and forms part of the gatway into the historical core of Philadelphia. Landscaping includes old gum trees as well as the Eeufees stone commemorating the Groot Trek.

Remnant of the historic farm Clara Anna Fontein, one of the oldest farms in the Tygerberg area. Main house was rebuilt in the 1920s. Intact farm werf layout and well preserved historic tree lines/avenues. Forms part of othe Durbanville Hills Cultural Landscape.
Kanonkop with its cannon, formed part of the historical signaling system at the 17th and 18th century Cape. Significant landmark qualities with the Durbanville Hills.
Contemporary alterations with significant additions to the earlier farmstead resulting in a reinterpretation of the werf and layout. Remains a scenic contributor to the cultural landscape.

Loosely laid out werf. T-shaped homestead (Victorianised). Varied typologies present in the werf. New additions are not intrusive and do not detract of significance.

Mid 18th century farmstead. Well presented swartland farm predominantly Victorian style, but containing earlier fabric. Remants of historical tree plantings framing the historical werf. Good representative example. Contribtues to the continuing cultural landscape.

Mid 20th century subdivision of Contermanskloof. Forms a significant backdrop to Contermanskloof farmstead. Associated signficance with regards to Kanonkop.
Irregular werf with older component along the NE edge. Newer infill buildings in the vernacular style arranged on the SW edge, forming an irregular square werf. Readaption for holiday accommodation.

19th century sudivision of an earliere farm. Fairly good example of swartland werf with somewhat altered historical buildings, but high degree of legibility. Contributes to the continuing cultural landscape.

hpoz.about: The City of Cape Town, in order to fulfil its obligation to sustainable development, must promote economic and social development, as well as promoting the conservation and protection of the natural and cultural environment. The City of Cape Town is a competent local authority in terms of the NHRA. The identification and management of Grade III heritage resources are the responsibility of the competent local authority.The Municipal Planning By-Law (2015) (MPBL) was enacted by the City of Cape Town from 1 July 2015 and replaced 2013 Cape Town Zoning Scheme. Included in this By-Law is the concept of overlay zonings. The overlay zoning provides a mechanism to designate either city-wide or localised development management rules to deal with specific concerns, over and above the provisions of a base zoning. One such overlay zone is the Heritage Protection Overlay (HPO). The Heritage Protection Overlay within the DMS is the mechanism for the protection of heritage places and areas that are considered conservation worthy in terms of the City’s heritage strategies and the National Heritage Resources Act (Act 25 of 1999) (NHRA). Schedule 3, Division II Item 18 states: “All Heritage Protection Overlay Zones as published in the Provincial Gazette are deemed to be heritage areas in accordance with the NHRA.”

Robben Island Prison is an inactive prison on Robben Island in Table Bay, 6.9 kilometers (4.3 mi) west of the coast of Bloubergstrand, Cape Town, South Africa. Nobel Laureate and former President of South Africa Nelson Mandela was imprisoned there for 18 of the 27 years he served behind bars before the fall of apartheid. Since then, three former inmates of the prison (Mandela, Kgalema Motlanthe, and Jacob Zuma) have gone on to become President of South Africa.
It is a South African National Heritage Site as well as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

stories.title: Hyaena dens and hand-axes
stories.text:
Long before the dunes had their present shape, the ground just north of where Koeberg now stands was a place of bones. Duinefontein 1 is a set of fossil hyaena burrows. A little away from it, Duinefontein 2 holds Middle Pleistocene animal bones together with a few rare stone tools of the Acheulian, the hand-axe tradition of early humans.

Archaeologists who excavated it date it to roughly 400,000 to 250,000 years ago. It is among the oldest traces of people anywhere on this coast, and it lies under the same sand you can see from the Koeberg beach road.

stories.title: Middens in the reserve
stories.text:
Wikipedia says shell middens inside today's Blaauwberg Nature Reserve date back about 15,000 years. It gives no source, the sentence is marked 'citation needed', and no excavation report seen for this map confirms it, so treat the age as unproven. Off-road driving destroyed some middens before the reserve stopped vehicles reaching the beach. SAHRIS lists dozens of archaeological sites between Blouberg and Melkbos, and the City's inventory adds more.

In a sand blowout on Blaauwberg farm, about 1.5 m below the surface, Jonathan Kaplan counted some eighty Later Stone Age tools. Most were of fine silcrete, with grindstones, hammerstones, an anvil, small pieces of red ochre and part of a bored digging-stick weight. Limpet shells there link the camp to a sea more than 3 km away. No pottery was found, so the camp is probably older than 2,000 years.

stories.title: Herders at the shore
stories.text:
About two thousand years ago, sheep and pottery came to the southern African coast, and with them the herders whom the Dutch would later know as the Khoe. Melkbos was a good place to be: the rocks offered rich shellfish, and people came back again and again.

Middens under today's Atlantic Beach estate are dated to about AD 700–750 and AD 1050. A midden at Erf 164 in the old village formed in the mid-600s, and its excavators read it as left by pastoralist people. The archaeologists say Melkbosstrand has produced 'an extremely high density' of pre-colonial burials, most likely because so many people lived well off the shore.

stories.title: The woman beneath Fifth Avenue
stories.text:
In March 2010 builders on Erf 164, a house plot on Fifth Avenue in old Melkbos, struck shell and bone. The archaeologists who were called in found a woman, over sixty years old, buried in a grave cut into an older shell midden. Radiocarbon dates put her burial close to the end of the 8th century AD, some 150 years after the midden formed.

A 19th-century foundation had been laid right next to her, missing her skull by centimetres. She is one of many: the national catalogue of Holocene skeletons lists 22 burials from Melkbosstrand and 20 from Blaauwberg, and a separate rescue excavation was needed for human remains found at No. 39 on the same avenue.

stories.title: Autshumao and the Goringhaikona
stories.text:
The first people documented at Bloubergstrand were the Goringhaikona, led by Autshumao, whom the Dutch called 'Harry die Strandloper'. In 1629 an English ship took him to Java to learn English; on his return he handled letters for passing ships, and is remembered as the Cape's first postmaster. His niece Krotoa would later become the interpreter between the Khoe and the Dutch.

Inland, the grazing lands from the Blaauwberg to the Groene Kloof hills belonged to the Cochoqua, the largest Khoe group of the Cape's west coast.

stories.title: Fires across the bay
stories.text:
On 6 April 1652 Jan van Riebeeck landed the Drommedaris and the Goede Hoope in Table Bay, with the Reijger following a day later. The Dutch East India Company founded a refreshment station for its ships between the Netherlands and Batavia, and the Cape began.

From his new fort, Van Riebeeck looked north across the water to the Blaauwberg shore, and wrote in his journal of the people already living there.

quote.text: many fires burning in the mountains on the opposite side of the bay

image.credit: Charles Davidson Bell, 'Landing of Van Riebeeck at the Cape of Good Hope in 1652' (before 1851)

stories.title: Slagtersveld, behind the Blaauwe berg
stories.text: In the Company's time the whole country behind the hill had a blunt name: Slagtersveld, the butchers' field. The governors sent hunters out on their behalf to shoot game 'behind the Blaauwe berg'. Farms with names that still sound on the map, such as Zoute Rivier, Duine Fontein, Brakke Fontein and Groene Kloof, were settled and worked between 1652 and 1795.

sources.title: HIA, proposed sand mine on the farm Brakke Kuyl Nos. 38 and 39, Blouberg

stories.title: De Kleine Post at Groene Kloof
stories.text:
The 'green gorge' in the hills north-east of Melkbos was Cochoqua grazing land. The VOC set up a cattle post there in 1697, and from 1701 a small garrison, De Kleine Post, kept the Company's herds until 1791. The Company never sold the land.

In 1778 the soldier-explorer Robert Jacob Gordon drew the post, shown here: a werf of low thatched buildings and kraals in a fold of open country.

Near the Modder River, archaeologists later found a camp with stone tools, red ochre and the remains of a wooden bowl made of bamboo, a wood not found at the Cape. They think it came from the East, and was in Khoe or San hands soon after 1652.

image.credit: Robert Jacob Gordon, 'View of the VOC cattle post, Groene Cloof', c. August 1778–1779 (Rijksmuseum)

stories.title: The loan farms
stories.text:
After 1700 the free burghers moved out over the sandveld. Kuiperskraal went to Hendrick Moller in 1702, and Sondagsfontein to Elsje van Suurwaarden in 1705. Ganzekraal 'bij de Groene Cloov' was granted to Martin Mecklenburg in 1709. Brakke Kuyl was granted around 1714. By 1767 Keert de Koe, the farm under Groot Oliphantskop whose name means 'turn the cow', belonged to Petrus de Witt; old fabric still survives on its werf.

Their werven, avenues and graveyards are still scattered through the farmland between the coast and the Koeberg hills.

stories.title: The farm Melkbosch
stories.text: The town takes its name from the milkbush (Euphorbia) on the dunes. Wikipedia describes the old farmhouse Melkbosch as the first farm the VOC established outside Cape Town, still standing though damaged by fire (unverified — the article gives no reference). The City's heritage inventory records the farm landscape of Klein Melkbosch from the 17th–18th century. The bay itself was known as Losperd's Bay.

stories.title: Gordon draws the coast
stories.text:
On 28 July 1777 the soldier-explorer Robert Jacob Gordon stood on Robben Island and drew the whole west coast in one long panorama, from the Table Mountain chain to the Blaauwberg and the hills beyond. Around 1788 he mapped Table Bay with its coastline 'from Kampsbaai to Lospertsbaai': the old name of the bay at Melkbos.

His drawings, now in the Rijksmuseum, are the earliest close views of this shore.

stories.title: A French fleet off the coast
stories.text: According to Wikipedia, a French fleet under Admiral Bailli de Suffren anchored just north of Melkbosstrand in 1781, when French troops helped garrison the Cape (1781–1783). Wrecks of many periods lie along this coast.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Melkbosstrand (History)

stories.title: The Damhuis
stories.text: On Melkbos bay stands the Damhuis, a late 18th-century fisherman's house and the last of its kind in the area besides Ons Huisie at Blouberg. When the township was laid out in 1924 it was still one of the only buildings here. Today it is a beach restaurant.

stories.title: Duinefontein, the dune spring
stories.text:
In 1799 the farm Duinefontein, a spring among the dunes north of Melkbos, was granted to Hermanus Dempers. He was a brickmaker, and in 1790 he was made adjutant of the burgher cavalry with the rank of cornet. In September 1811 he complained to the government that tenants were cutting wood on his land. When it was surveyed for a quitrent grant in 1834, the diagram showed no buildings at all, only a stock kraal.

Later owners were the carpenter Pieter Wahl, who died in 1877; Pieter Joseph Vink, from 1892; and the Loubsers, from 1926. The Electricity Commission bought the farm in 1967. Family lore says a Vink once came upon treasure washed ashore at Blaauwberg Strand, but that is a story, not a record. The Verweys of nearby Rietdam and Oliphantskop farmed here until the early 1960s.

stories.title: A ride in the mist
stories.text: In May 1804, in the last years of Dutch rule, the Batavian officer W.B.E. Paravicini di Capelli rode north from Cape Town towards Saldanha Bay. His journal records breakfast at Riet Vallei and the turn-off to the Koebergen, and the valley of Groene Cloof smelling of growing things.

quote.text: through the valley of Blaauwberg and the Blaauwberg, which was obscured by the mist
quote.by: W.B.E. Paravicini di Capelli, journal, 17 May 1804 (Van Riebeeck Society, 1965)

stories.title: The landing at Losperd's Bay
stories.text: On 4 January 1806 a British fleet of 63 ships, carrying about 7,000 troops, anchored off Robben Island. The surf at Losperd's Bay was heavy. Commodore Popham scuttled a small merchant ship to make a breakwater, and on 6 and 7 January General David Baird's two brigades came ashore at Melkbosstrand. Thirty-six men of the 93rd Highlanders drowned when their boat capsized.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Battle of Blaauwberg

stories.title: The morning after the battle
stories.text:
On 8 January the British met General Janssens's Batavian line in the dunes east of the Kleinberg. The Waldeck battalion fell back and the Highland brigade charged. Baird set up his headquarters at Riet Vlei. The British lost Captain Andrew Foster and 14 men killed, with 180 wounded; the Batavian side about 337 killed, wounded and missing. More than two hundred war graves have never been found.

The chaplain Henry Martyn crossed the hill the same day. He found Captain Foster dead and some two hundred wounded at the burgher Justinus Keer's farm. A drunken Highlander insisted Martyn was a Frenchman.

Cape Town capitulated on 10 January, and the colony on 18 January. Five days after the battle Baird ordered the Khoe 'Hottentot Corps' re-formed under Major John Graham of the 93rd.

quote.text: All whom we approached cried out instantly for water

stories.title: Mamre
stories.text:
On 23 March 1808 the Governor, the Earl of Caledon, granted De Groene Kloof, Louwskloof and Cruywagenskraal to the Moravian mission. The founders, Kohrhammer and Schmitt, gathered Khoe families around the old Company post. The Khoe captain Hans Clapmuts and some seventy followers lived at Louwskloof; he joined the congregation in 1839, aged about 110 and blind.

By 1835 there were some 700 homes. A school opened in 1833, a horse mill around 1830 and the watermill in 1844, and a steam engine arrived in 1879. The village was renamed Mamre in 1854. Its church, completed in 1818 according to the 2012 heritage study (Wikipedia gives 1816), is among the oldest still standing in the country. In 1900 Mamre founded the Coloured Political Association, described there as the first political organisation for coloured people.

image.credit: Watermill, Mamre mission station — photo by KNewman1 (2009)

stories.title: The Stadlers of Blouberg
stories.text: Shortly after the battle, Frederick Louis Stadler became owner of almost all the farmland that is now Bloubergstrand. Ons Huisie was his first dwelling; Thomas Bowler drew it in 1853. His descendants were among the founders of the village, and the old street names still remember Baird, Janssens, Popham and the Stadlers.

image.credit: Ons Huisie, Bloubergstrand — photo by Debbielouise (2012)

sources.title: Wikipedia — Bloubergstrand (History)

stories.title: Ganzekraal and the hunting lodge
stories.text:
At the northern edge of the story lies Ganzekraal. The Company kept a cattle post there in 1724, and from 1791 the Van Reenen brothers farmed it. They were the family who joined the expedition of 1790–91 searching for survivors of the wrecked East Indiaman Grosvenor. Lady Anne Barnard visited and sketched the house in 1798 or 1799. It burnt down in 1965.

Inland, at Groote Post, Lord Charles Somerset kept a hunting place while he was Governor, from 1814 to 1828.

sources.title: The Heritage Portal — Ganzekraal homestead, Western Cape

stories.title: Philadelphia
stories.text: The farmers of the Koeberg did not want to ride all the way to Durbanville for church. They acquired part of a farm and in 1858 began building their own Dutch Reformed church; the parish was established in 1863. Its name, from Revelation, means 'brotherly love'. The little village, with its grid of streets lined in blue gums, may be the smallest formally laid-out 'kerkdorp' in the Cape. Along the old Darling road, a blue-gum avenue still marks the way north.

stories.title: A cross on the rocks
stories.text: The large wooden cross on the Blouberg promontory was put up in memory of Heather Bam, who drowned off the point in 1911. Later the children's author Mollie Lochner lived in the house at the end of Stadler Road.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Bloubergstrand (History)

stories.title: A mine off Cape Town
stories.text: On 26 May 1917 the Spanish mail steamer Carlos de Eizaguirre, on her way from Cádiz to Manila, struck a mine near Cape Town and sank in about four minutes. The mine had been laid by the German raider Wolf. Accounts of the dead differ: Wikipedia's article on the Wolf gives 134 dead and 24 survivors; its list of 1917 shipwrecks gives 84 of 108 aboard, or 126 of 150. A 2026 maritime heritage study for the Waban cable (TerraMare) is reported to place the wreck about 5.5 km north of the new cable landing at Duynefontein; that report could not be opened to check this, so the wreck is not yet on the map.

stories.title: Melkbosch Strand is laid out
stories.text: In 1924 the Cape Lands Development Company laid out a seaside township on the old Losperd's Bay land. At the time there was little here besides the Damhuis, a few holiday houses and the post office. A few small cottages from the 1930s still stand along Beach Road among later houses.

stories.title: Watch on Blaauwberg Hill
stories.text:
During the Second World War a radar station, a lookout and a mess room were built on Blaauwberg Hill, watching the sea approaches to Cape Town. The buildings still stand in the nature reserve.

The war reached this water. In July 1942 the American freighter Oklahoman ran aground on Dassen Island in fog. On 7 October 1942 U-172 sank the Chickasaw City off Cape Town, the first ship sunk by a U-boat off the South African coast. Within two days the Firethorn, Pantelis and Clan MacTavish followed.

stories.text: The City of Cape Town's 1953 aerial photograph is the earliest that covers Melkbos. It shows a small seaside settlement among farm fields and dune bush. Press play to watch the coast change, photograph by photograph, to January 2026.

stories.title: A cable to Europe
stories.text: In 1961 Melkbosstrand became the landing point of the SAT-1 copper telephone cable to Sesimbra in Portugal. It was replaced by the SAT-2 fibre-optic cable in 1992, and Melkbos remains a landing point for the SAT-3/WASC system.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Melkbosstrand (History)

stories.title: Mamre, 1962
stories.text: In December 1962 Looksmart Ngudle and Denis Goldberg helped organise an Umkhonto we Sizwe training camp at Mamre, later recognised as the first such camp inside South Africa. It was abandoned early after Security Police attention.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Mamre, South Africa (History)

stories.title: Atlantis
stories.text: Atlantis was founded in 1976 by the government under the Group Areas Act, as a town for Cape Town's Coloured community. It was built on the farms Melkpost, Hartebeeskraal and Witzand, with incentives to bring in industry such as Atlantis Diesel Engines. By the early 1980s some fifty industrialists employed people from nearly 8,000 households; the area later declined and has since been revived.

sources.title: AIA, optic fibre cable Melkbos to Yzerfontein (2013) — Atlantis
Wikipedia — Atlantis, South Africa

stories.title: Koeberg
stories.text: Construction of Koeberg, Africa's only nuclear power station, began in 1976 with the French company Framatome, on land that had been the farm Duinefontein. It was damaged by explosives in December 1982 while still under construction, before any fuel was loaded. Unit 1 was connected to the grid on 4 April 1984 and Unit 2 on 25 July 1985. Housing built for the Koeberg and Atlantis Diesel Engines workers shaped much of modern Melkbos.

image.credit: Koeberg Nuclear Power Station — photo by Paul Scott (2010)

sources.title: Wikipedia — Koeberg Nuclear Power Station

stories.title: One city
stories.text: When the metropolitan boundaries were redrawn after 1994, Melkbosstrand became part of the City of Cape Town's Blaauwberg region. The nature conservation zone to the south and Koeberg's buffer to the north have kept it a seaside village.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Melkbosstrand

stories.title: Blaauwberg Nature Reserve
stories.text: Proclaimed in 2007, the reserve protects 1,445 hectares of strandveld, renosterveld and sand fynbos, the ancient shell middens and the 1806 battlefield. It is one of the few places from which two World Heritage Sites can be seen at once: Table Mountain and Robben Island.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Blaauwberg Nature Reserve

stories.title: Atlantis, green industry
stories.text: In 2018 the Atlantis industrial area was designated a Special Economic Zone focused on green technology. Factories there now make wind-turbine towers and other renewable-energy components.

sources.title: Wikipedia — Atlantis, South Africa (Revitalization)

stories.title: Duynefontein, the cable shore
stories.text: Just south-east of Koeberg, Duynefontein received national environmental authorisation in 2025 for a possible new nuclear power station; the project still awaits further approvals. Its beach at Van Riebeeckstrand is now a landing point for subsea cables: ACE and 2Africa, and in 2026 heritage studies were filed for the Waban and Wamkelekile cables, which will run through the same sleeves beneath the dunes.

stories.title: Mamre's werf, restored
stories.text: On 8 July 2026 the Mamre werf was handed over to the builders for an eighteen-month rescue and conservation project. The church came first. Crumbling lime plaster from earlier repairs was cut away, and re-thatching began, this time with a fire-retardant blanket. Termites and borer beetle were found deep in the walls. The old shop, the barn, the Langhuis and the bakehouse are next, and the project is due to finish in January 2028.

stories.title: Melkbos today
stories.text: The latest City aerial photograph, taken in January 2026, shows a town of about 12,000 people along seven kilometres of white beach, with Blouberg to the south and Atlantis to the north-east. Every layer of its story is still here: the hyaena dens under Koeberg, the middens in the dunes, a woman's grave under a garden on Fifth Avenue, the Damhuis on the rocks, and the cannon on the foreshore that remembers 1806.
